1:
Who the righteous man is divides the tile at once. Gill guards the verb, since the perishing is of the outward man only and cannot be eternal for one who believes; Henry puts the same in a phrase, that righteousness delivers from the sting of death but not from the stroke, and takes the word to mark the loss the world sustains rather than any undoing of the dead. Ellicott gives it a date, hearing the words as written in the anticipation or the actual presence of a king's persecution of the prophets, with the singular pointing to a few conspicuous sufferers who had vexed their souls to death over the evils around them. Clarke goes further than any: there is an emphasis in the Hebrew that seems to point out a particular person, and since he holds that few places in this book do not intend Christ he takes it of the Just One, the merciful men gathered after him being the apostles and the primitive Christians, and the evil to come the destruction by the Romans.

Clarke also presses the verb itself. Its root describes cattle straying from one pasture to another, and he takes the Latin word behind the English in its grammatical sense of going through, so that the righteous man passes through life and passes before others into the eternal world, as the older English said of a man that he went out of sight or fared forth.

Henry stays with the world's inattention, which he thinks the graver fault. The death of good men is to be laid to heart more than common deaths; the removal is in compassion to those taken, called into the ark before the deluge, and in wrath to those left, since it is a sign that God intends war when he calls home his ambassadors. Wesley says only that few or none are duly affected by so sad a sign of displeasure.

The second verse turns on a question of number. Clarke would emend it, dividing one word to recover the perfect man, reading the verb as singular on the authority of manuscripts and versions, and observing that the words each one supplied by the translators may then be spared; he cites a parallel restoration made by the same method in a psalm, and applies the whole to a spirit walking on in conscious existence after death. Wesley keeps the text and explains the shift as a sudden change of number very frequent in the prophets. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch keep both numbers, Ellicott rendering the last clause as everyone who has walked straight before him, that is, taken the straight path of duty.

On the peace itself they agree and enlarge. Gill lists what the righteous enters: the God of peace, the Prince of peace, the Spirit whose fruit is peace, with no sin within and no tempter without. Ellicott finds the verse notable as the brighter side of Israel's dim thoughts about the life behind the veil, and states the antithesis the chapter will close on: for the righteous there is peace in death as in life, for the wicked in neither. All take the bed for the grave, Henry adding that it is made in darkness and is the quieter for it, and that those who rise from it will rise refreshed.
3:
The summons is to a bar. Gill has the wicked called up to hear their character and their doom, Henry sets them at the bar as arraigned, Wesley brings them to God's tribunal for sentence. What their parentage means divides them. Ellicott allows that the sorceress may be purely figurative but thinks she may also point to real female soothsayers, and says the same of the adulterer. Wesley makes the descent one of imitation, not propagation, their dispositions suiting a bastard brood better than the seed of Abraham. Henry makes it moral outright, since sin is itself sorcery and adultery, a departure from God and a dealing with the devil. Keil and Delitzsch note the common practice of indicating a man's character by naming his father.

Where the speaker stands is a sharper question. Keil and Delitzsch have the prophet looking back from the standpoint of the captivity, addressing the people of the exile about an idolatry handed down from their ancestors, though taking his colours from his own day. Ellicott argues the other way from the details: the slaying of children leaves not the slightest trace of revival among the exiles or after the return, and the scenery, the torrent-stream and the clefts of the rock, belongs distinctively to Palestine. Gill, Henry and Wesley take the generation contemporary with the prophet.

On the mockery the voices converge. Ellicott calls the question one of indignant scorn whose implied answer is that the mockers derided the servants of God and in that God himself, the wide mouth and drawn tongue being the natural symbols of derision. Gill agrees the sport is not so much against the messengers as against the Lord whose they are; Henry makes it Jerusalem's measure-filling sin and observes that they would not have treated a gentleman's servant on an errand with so little civility.

The verb for inflaming draws out the best of Ellicott, who illustrates it from the derivation of fanatic as one heated about a shrine, and says no word better describes the orgiastic excitement of heathen rites; he would read among the terebinths rather than with idols, and notes that under every green tree is nearly a formula, the tree itself becoming an object of the cultus. Gill offers two renderings, images of oaken wood or the mighty ones, and turns both into an indictment of Rome and the kingdoms she is said to consort with. Wesley keeps it plain, that they lusted after the idols and were mad upon them, and takes the clefts to have been chosen for shade or for dark vaults.

The smooth stones bring out Clarke's antiquarianism. He assembles a dossier on the worship of rude consecrated stones, tracing it to the pillar anointed at Bethel which gave the Phoenician baetyls their name: a Church Father confessing that before his conversion he would flatter and petition any smooth stone he found smeared with oil, another using the worshipper of every smooth stone as a proverb, a Greek character-sketch of the superstitious man stopping in the street to pour oil from his phial and kneel, and a living parallel in the sacred stones of India. Ellicott independently reaches the same Phoenician name and connects the cult with the reproductive powers of nature, then presses the irony: the true portion of Israel was God, and these chose a fetish instead. Gill notes a play in the Hebrew between smooth stones and portion that will not come into English. Henry says they would worship a carved stone set up for nothing but a way-mark, and loved their idols better than their children, their own tables being robbed to supply the altars. Wesley adds that the devil is God's ape, idolaters using the very rites God prescribed for himself. Ellicott would render the closing question not as receiving comfort but as being quiet in spite of this.
7:
The bed on the high mountain is read by all as the place of idol worship, Ellicott observing that once idolatry is adultery the bed follows naturally, Wesley calling it the altar. What stands behind the door is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch take the remembrance for the declaration that the Lord alone is God, the text that belonged on the door-post and has been pushed out of sight. Clarke makes it the image of a household god, set privately in defiance of a curse the law pronounces on whoever puts a graven image in a secret place; Wesley says the heathen placed their tutelary gods there to have them in view going out and coming in. Ellicott reports the memorial text as the common explanation and calls it tenable, but thinks an idolatrous symbol substituted for it equally possible.

Gill reads the passage as an allegory of Rome, finding the seven hills in the lofty mountain, crucifixes in the household memorials, and the last anointing in the ointment. Who that king is divides the rest. Ellicott notes that a single letter's change would give Molech and allows that this may be the sense as the text stands, but judges the Assyrian more natural, and reads the ointment and perfumes as treasures lavished to buy that alliance. Wesley has the king of Assyria named by eminency, and marks where the prophet turns from idolatry to confidence in princes; Keil and Delitzsch make the two reciprocal. Clarke will have Assyria or Egypt and explains the present, since in the east no one visits a great man empty-handed, so the verb for visiting came to mean making a gift.

The weariness of the long way is taken by Ellicott as the length of the journey, the embassies to Assyria and Babylon, and he re-renders the next clause: not that there is no hope but that there is no result, Judah refusing to admit the negotiations were fruitless. Clarke would reverse the sentence: a manuscript leaves the negative unpointed as suspect, and two parallel places show a desperate resolve to go on at all hazards, so he reads that she said there is hope. Keil and Delitzsch keep the text and gloss the word from Arabic, where the sense of hoping grows out of stretching and drawing out while despairing is literally a drawing in.

On the fear behind it Keil and Delitzsch are blunt: from the fear of man, and of mortal men with no real power, Israel gave up the fear of God. Ellicott calls the alliance an acted lie and hears the question about silence half-pityingly, since long-suffering had been mistaken for apathy. Wesley says the forbearance meant to oblige them to love him was abused. Clarke proposes another emendation, reading not even of old but and winked, on the authority of twenty-three manuscripts and the ancient versions, and holds that a reading so confirmed admits of no doubt.

The righteousness God threatens to declare is taken ironically by Ellicott, as the righteousness that is none, though a slight alteration adopted by many gives my righteousness, which Clarke reports from the versions. Keil and Delitzsch keep the text and press the irony hardest: the word cannot mean salvation here but only what Israel in its blindness took for righteousness. Of the companies called on to save her, Ellicott says the word is used contemptuously of a crowd of gods brought in by confluent idolatry; Gill takes them for images and departed saints; Henry heaps idol-gods and confederate troops together and lets the wind have them, since they have made themselves chaff and vanity is both what they are and what shall take them away. Against them stands the promise Keil and Delitzsch mark as turning the chapter, that whoever trusts shall inherit the land and the holy mountain.
14:
Who gives the order to clear the road is disputed four ways. Clarke points the verb as a first person future and makes it God speaking, since the verse closes with my people. Keil and Delitzsch hold the subject deliberately obscure, a heavenly cry whose crier is not to be identified, and note that the appeal recurs once in each of the three books of these prophecies. Ellicott hears a voice behind the prophet renewing the herald's cry of an earlier chapter; Wesley expects a man whom God will raise up to say it, Gill an apocalyptic scene.

On the great title all agree, each taking a different measure of it. Keil and Delitzsch make the mercy the ground of the voice being heard at all, since the Holy One has a manifestation of glory above and of grace below, the heaven of heavens not too great for him nor a heart too small. Ellicott states it as the central comfort, that the infinitely Great One cares for the infinitely little, the greatness of lowliness shown in Christ reflecting a permanent law of divine government.

The half-verse about the failing spirit divides method from method. Keil and Delitzsch work it by grammar, rejecting the sense the early translators gave the verb as one that cannot be established, and dismissing two modern renderings on the form of the verb. Clarke says the learned have taken great pains to little purpose here and settles it by two passages of the Psalms he prints as parallel, then distinguishes the animal life from the immortal spirits and notes an ancient version reading a resurrection into it. Ellicott puts it in a sentence: the time in which God contends has limits, or the souls he made would be consumed and his purpose frustrated.

Covetousness as the cause is where Clarke breaks from everyone. He would read not the iniquity of his covetousness but his iniquity for a short time, following the Greek, and calls the Latin rendering all others follow quite beside the purpose. Ellicott keeps the text, gives the word literally as gain, and makes it the root-evil from which the rest sprang. Henry sharpens it: those who worshipped no images were carried away by this spiritual idolatry, which is making money the god, and no wonder the people were covetous when their watchmen were. Gill turns the reproach forward onto ministers of the reformed churches, who seek benefices and pluralities and take oversight of the flock for lucre.

Whose ways God has seen is smaller. Ellicott reports both the evil ways just described and the way of repentance, preferring the first, God presenting himself as healer to those the path had wounded; Clarke thinks these verses refer to the restoration from captivity. On the created fruit of the lips Clarke takes the sacrifice of praise and extends the peace to Jew and Gentile; Ellicott includes Jews in the city, Jews in exile, and Gentiles whose distance was spiritual. Wesley notes that the doubled word marks certainty.

The close is a refusal. Ellicott makes the healing conditional, since accepting peace requires calmness and for men whose thoughts seethe with evil it is impossible; he marks the recurring watchword as closing a section, suggests the sea in view may be the Dead Sea casting up its deposits, and notices that the manuscripts vary between my God, God, and the Lord God, as if copyists had shrunk from the prophet's boldness in claiming God as his own. Clarke reports the same variation and ties the verse back to the promise, from which the impenitent are excluded. Henry has the terrors of conscience casting up mire that makes such men a burden to themselves, and says God has said it and the world cannot unsay it. Gill adds that prosperity is no exception, the peace refused being inward and everlasting.
